beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You cannot really share an agent.
beats.got: Sharing an agent isn't one thing. There are four options and I'm supposed to pick one.

beats.trigger: Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to something and did not use it.
beats.got: This is about licences nobody uses, which is my turf. I can name two of those straight away.

beats.trigger: **Test** the switch assumptions and leave with one named conversation and one test
beats.got: Five verbs and no number. I can't tell what it costs or what it saves.

beats.trigger: What would you want them to have: your folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack?
beats.got: Four ways to share. I don't have an agent, a folder or skills, so I'd have to borrow someone else's setup.

beats.trigger: Hold the impulse. Then start with the teammate's work.
beats.got: Start from the colleague's job, not from my tool. That's reasonable, but it's a long intro for it.

beats.trigger: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: Claude writes a file naming a person, how they work now and an outcome I could observe. 'Observable' is the useful word.

beats.trigger: *"Share the whole agent"* is a vendor pitch and is NOT on the list.
beats.got: Pick the option by what it does for the person's result, not because it fits our infrastructure. They call the 'whole agent' option a vendor pitch, which I agree with.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: Two files done. Next step is the obstacles.

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: Find the one obstacle that matters, then write the plans.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Find the one obstacle that, once removed, makes the others easier. That's how I'd cut a cost list down to the driver.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: The tech plan looks done while nobody owns it. I've seen that in three programmes. It's an accountability gap.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact
beats.got: Next is testing the assumptions.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses until tested.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: What would have to be true for them to drop what they use today? That's a business-case question and I can ask it.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: A pre-mortem. Imagine it failed, then act on the strongest reason. I like that it names the risk before I have to.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Choosing a tool because it fits our stack is shopping. Choosing it because it moves a result is design.

beats.trigger: One law decides whether a sharing plan works.
beats.got: A claim of one law. Let's see if they back it up.

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: Licences activated and people actually using them get reported as one figure. That's what I see in every rollout report.

beats.trigger: The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.
beats.got: Good analysis, no decision, because the leaders hadn't done the work. I know that meeting. It's a story and not a number, and it's from one company.

beats.trigger: They had not spent any of their own weeks inside it.
beats.got: The people who did the work took it in. The people who only got the report didn't.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy. Accountability doesn't. I think it means someone has to own what the agent does, and it's a bit abstract.

beats.trigger: The right choice is the one that fits the week your teammate already has.
beats.got: Each option asks something different of the person. Choose the one that fits their week.

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.
beats.got: The competitor is the spreadsheet or gut call they use now. The switch needs to land where they look, be right first time, and be vouched for by someone they trust.

beats.trigger: Send them a message today and ask for twenty minutes of their week.
beats.got: Concrete and small: one person, twenty minutes, one question about how they work today. I can do that.

beats.trigger: Run this in the same session.
beats.got: A wrap-up prompt, nothing new.

beats.trigger: Test the switch, not the solution.
beats.got: Six points. The ones I keep are job first, name the roles, and test the switch.

beats.trigger: Bring what your Monday contact said, in their own words.
beats.got: Evidence from a real conversation counts, not the plan. Fine by me.

beats.trigger: Module 8 puts the agent to work on the building.
beats.got: Next module is the agent building things.

take_homes: Switched-on access and actual use are two numbers. Ask for the second one before I sign off on any rollout.
Before buying or sharing a tool, ask what the person does today and what would have to be true for them to drop it.
Put the technical plan and the people plan side by side. If the roles have no names, nobody owns it yet.

monday.move: Ask my controller for 20 minutes to see how she writes the month-end variance commentary today, and ask what would have to be true for her to use an agent for it.
monday.stop_condition: If she says the current way works and nothing would make her switch, I drop it.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data.

misconception.why: Access versus absorption fits what I see with licences: bought, switched on, not used. So a licence alone is not the capability. But the module never gave a cost, a payback or a number, and I still can't say what it costs per month for 40 people. I'm half moved.

one_line: Good on why rollouts stall, and the 'who owns this' point is useful. But there wasn't one number in it, so I still can't take it to the board.
